In order for ALS to be easily adopted, the light levels during periods of low use should not affect road users’ safety, security, or visibility. Evidence-based research is required not only to determine the light levels to dim to but also the times during which it should be dimmed. • Due to fact that ALS have only been installed recently and tested in limited areas, there has not been much time to evaluate their effects on safety and security. However, there are systems that have been in place for over 3 years and thus a before-and-after analysis is required to determine their effectiveness. • It is extremely important to understand the barriers to adoption of ALS technology from the points of view of all stakeholders, such as transportation agencies, road users, lighting designers, local government, and electric utilities. It is also important to get feedback from towns and cities that have already implemented ALS to document the information that can help other potential adopters. 30 3 Technology Enablers To enable adaptive lighting, an algorithm is required that determines the behavior of the lighting system. This algorithm can generally be considered a schedule of lighting level, timing, and duration of lighting system changes. The inputs to the algorithm include factors already identified: traffic volume, intersection presence, pedestrian usage, and presence of parked vehicles. The algorithm can also consider the needs for the area in terms of humans, animals, and flora. The technological requirements of an ALS are a dimming-capable luminaire and control mechanisms at each pole location and the central controller/host. The individual and host controllers are commonly coupled through a wireless mesh or cellular communications, although other networking approaches such as powerline carriers and wired networks have also been used. In addition, two policy-based requirements must be met to implement ALS: (1) the controlling agency must identify an adaptive lighting specification to define when and how the lights can be changed; and (2) an adaptive lighting tariff for the lighting system must be negotiated with the utility to capture the energy and financial savings. The use of SSL, a control system, and a central management software system are key to success. Adaptive lighting necessitates two primary characteristics: (1) instant on and off, and (2) dimming. Instant on and off capabilities allow lighting to be instantaneously reactive to changing lighting needs on the roadway. Dimming capabilities of the lighting system are also needed to allow the lighting level to be adjusted in intensity rather than turning the system off and on. The response of the system is critical to the changing nature of the roadway. These instant on/off and the ease of dimming requirements are both inherent only in LED systems.
